analysis_unit.notes: Pooled corpus of positive and negative free-text comments about the Red report style across multiple oncology scenarios.

summary.overall_impression: The Red report style was often valued for being structured, explicit, and clinically useful. Oncologists repeatedly liked the presence of bottom-line summaries, practical recommendations, patient-specific reasoning, and visible attempts to connect conclusions to evidence. At the same time, the most salient weaknesses were excessive length, visual heaviness, and citation practices that felt too opaque, hyperlink-dependent, or insufficiently specific. Comments also showed a recurring tension between appreciating practical communication aids and rejecting sections that felt overly conversational, overly patient-facing, or more inferential than necessary.
dominant_positive_themes: Clear structure with bottom-line summaries and headings
Practical, patient-specific recommendations and workflow-oriented guidance
Evidence-backed reasoning with explicit logic and cited support
dominant_negative_themes: Excessive length, redundancy, and too much text to sift through
Weak citation usability, specificity, and transparency
Tone or formatting choices that felt clunky, casual, visually noisy, or overly editorialized
dominant_improvement_requests: Shorten and tighten the report while preserving the answer and key reasoning
Make citations more specific, transparent, and compiled in a usable reference list
Reduce unnecessary sections, conversational phrasing, and formatting excess

positive_features.description: Many comments praised the presence of a clear up-front or end summary that made the main recommendation easy to identify quickly.
Respondents frequently described the reports as well organized, easy to read, and helped by headings, subheadings, or ordered presentation.
representative_examples: headings and subheadings were short and precise
number lists make it easy to read

positive_features.description: Across scenarios, clinicians often valued plain, readable language that made the content easier to digest.
The reports were often seen as useful when they translated literature into concrete next steps, recommendations, timelines, dosing guidance, or anticipated questions.
Clinicians appreciated when the output clearly incorporated the details of the presented case and tailored the recommendation accordingly.
representative_examples: narrowed down to personalize to this patient case

positive_features.description: Several comments praised the report for showing its logic, weighing risks and benefits, and making the reasoning behind conclusions more explicit.
representative_examples: explicit about what it's pulling out

positive_features.description: Positive comments often noted that conclusions felt supported by evidence, including mention of guidelines, trials, or concrete literature references.
representative_examples: specific citation of evidence to support final decision

positive_features.feature_label: Balanced presentation of pros and cons
positive_features.description: Some clinicians liked that the report acknowledged controversy, uncertainty, or competing options instead of presenting a one-sided answer.
A substantial subset of comments positively valued language that could be used to explain recommendations to patients in plain terms.
representative_examples: language for what you can share with the patient

positive_features.feature_label: Inclusion of quantitative detail when present
positive_features.description: When the report included statistics or outcome numbers, those details were seen as helpful and decision-relevant.

negative_features.description: The most repeated criticism was that the reports were too long, too wordy, or too dense for rapid clinical use.
representative_examples: too much text to sift through

negative_features.description: Comments described the reports as repetitive or padded with extra material that did not help answer the core question.
representative_examples: some added information are not very helpful

negative_features.description: Many respondents found the citation style hard to use because references appeared as hyperlinks or vague source labels rather than clearly inspectable citations.
representative_examples: citations are hyperlinks and can't quickly see

negative_features.feature_label: Insufficient citation specificity and reference detail
negative_features.description: Clinicians wanted to know exactly what study, guideline section, population, or document supported each statement, and often felt the report did not make that clear enough.
representative_examples: would like to know exactly where it is taken from
not enough references and explanation of the research
would like more description of what a link is

negative_features.description: Across scenarios, comments noted the absence of a compiled citation list at the end, even when inline references were present.
representative_examples: no citation/reference list at the end
nice to have a list at the end that is compiled

negative_features.feature_label: Too little hard data or weak evidence support
negative_features.description: Some clinicians felt the report lacked trial numbers, outcome statistics, stronger source selection, or enough evidence detail to support the recommendation confidently.
representative_examples: lack of specific numbers from trials

negative_features.description: Formatting choices such as excessive bolding, title-style citations, and visually heavy layouts were viewed as distracting.
Some respondents disliked the Q&A style or felt the structure delayed the answer rather than foregrounding it.
representative_examples: Q&A format is a bit clunky
doesn't get to the heart of the true question until the last paragraph
section should be moved to the top

negative_features.feature_label: Overly casual, conversational, or editorial tone
negative_features.description: A subset of clinicians reacted negatively to first-person phrasing, casual wording, buzzwords, parentheticals, or editorializing.

negative_features.feature_label: Patient-facing sections seen as unnecessary or oversimplified
negative_features.description: Although some clinicians liked patient-language sections, others thought these sections were too simplistic, unnecessary, or not appropriate for the intended user.
representative_examples: not sure if I like the 'what to say to patient' section
there are more nuances than what is listed

negative_features.description: Some comments suggested the report occasionally over-interpreted evidence, created false equivalence, or added inference beyond what was well supported.
representative_examples: false equivalence of pro and con data

improvement_requests.description: Respondents wanted a tighter report that surfaces the answer earlier and trims redundant or low-value content.
representative_examples: too much info for a quick look
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Excessive length, redundancy, and difficulty rapidly extracting the answer

improvement_requests.description: Clinicians repeatedly asked for a clear citation list at the end in addition to or instead of embedded hyperlinks.
representative_examples: citations need to be listed out
would want to see citations at the bottom
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Poor citation usability and inability to quickly inspect sources

improvement_requests.request_label: Make citations more specific and inspectable
improvement_requests.description: They wanted citations tied to exact claims, clearer study identification, and more detail about source type, journal, and relevance.
representative_examples: more description of what a link is
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Opaque evidence provenance and weak transparency of support for recommendations

improvement_requests.request_label: Include more hard data and trial numbers
improvement_requests.description: Many comments asked for quantitative outcomes, stronger statistics, and more explicit reporting of trial results and studied populations.
representative_examples: not as much hard data from references
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Insufficient evidentiary detail for assessing recommendation quality and applicability

improvement_requests.request_label: Use stronger and more relevant sources
improvement_requests.description: Some clinicians wanted better source selection, more guideline linkage, and clearer use of high-quality or specialty-relevant references.
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Concerns about source quality, completeness, and alignment with oncology practice

improvement_requests.description: Comments suggested putting the bottom line at the top and reducing the time required to reach the actionable answer.
representative_examples: section should be moved to the top
doesn't get to the heart of the true question until the last paragraph
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Delayed answer retrieval and suboptimal workflow fit

improvement_requests.request_label: Reduce formatting excess and visual clutter
improvement_requests.description: Respondents wanted cleaner presentation with less bolding, fewer visually noisy citation styles, and a lighter page layout.
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Reduced readability from distracting formatting choices

improvement_requests.request_label: Trim nonessential conversational or patient-facing sections
improvement_requests.description: Several clinicians wanted the report to drop unnecessary drafted messages, pushback language, or lay summaries that did not add value for them.
representative_examples: proposal to draft a message unnecessary
Do NOT like the lay summary
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Perceived overdelivery, tone mismatch, and clutter from low-value add-ons

mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.description: Practical recommendations were often appreciated, but some respondents felt the report crossed into unnecessary scripting, drafted messages, or patient-care decisions that should remain with the clinician.
representative_examples: practical recommendations appreciated, but drafted message or patient-care sections unnecessary

mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.description: Plain-language summaries for patients were highly valued by some clinicians and explicitly rejected by others who preferred to do their own phrasing or wanted more nuance.
representative_examples: was praised by some and disliked by others

mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.description: Comprehensiveness was sometimes experienced as a strength, but just as often as a burden when it increased scrolling, repetition, or delayed the core answer.
representative_examples: comprehensive and nuanced, but too long

mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.description: A more casual or ChatGPT-like voice helped readability for some, while others found the same style condescending, annoying, or insufficiently professional.
representative_examples: casual writing was helpful for one commenter but read as annoying or too conversational for others

interpretive_notes: The strongest pattern is not rejection of the report's reasoning, but dissatisfaction with how that reasoning is packaged: too much text, insufficiently inspectable citations, and too many optional sections.
Clinicians appear to value outputs that are simultaneously evidence-grounded and workflow-efficient: concise answer first, tailored reasoning second, and source transparency throughout.
The corpus suggests that citation usability is not just a formatting preference; it is closely tied to trust, perceived rigor, and the ability to verify applicability to the patient case.
Patient-facing language appears to be a true preference split rather than a uniformly good or bad feature, so this may need to be optional rather than standard.
data_quality_notes: Comments are short, fragmented, and sometimes telegraphic, so categories were consolidated across repeated wording patterns rather than treated as precise counts.
A small number of entries were blank or minimally informative.
Some positive comments contained embedded criticism such as 'good but long'; these were represented in both positive and mixed/negative sections where appropriate.
